clue.text: Youth always yearning for style

blocks.note: Peter Pan is the boy who never grows up, youth for ever
to ache for something is to yearn for it

explanation.surface: A young person forever longing to look stylish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Youth always' is one idea: Peter Pan, the boy who stays young for ever.
explanation.definitionFit: Panache is flamboyant confidence and dash in manner, a close synonym of flair or style.

clue.text: Judge joining you, say, in a drink? Witness shouldn't do that!

indicators.note: say means the word you is spoken, standing for a letter pronounced the same way
in places the judge and you together inside the drink

blocks.note: J is the abbreviation for judge
the letter U is pronounced like this word
perry is a drink like cider, made from pears

explanation.surface: A judge sharing a drink with a witness, followed by a warning that witnesses must avoid this.
explanation.walkthrough: Perry is fermented pear juice, the pear version of cider.
explanation.definitionFit: A witness under oath must not lie, and lying under oath is the crime this noun names.

clue.text: Trial for dark horse

blocks.note: night is the dark part of the day
a mare is a female horse

explanation.surface: A test run for a little-known racehorse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dark horse' is a fixed phrase for an unknown contender, but here the two words are clued separately.
explanation.definitionFit: A trial is an ordeal or source of distress, and a nightmare is a hugely unpleasant experience.

clue.text: Pick conservative paper

blocks.note: C is the abbreviation for Conservative
a ream is a quantity of paper, 500 sheets

explanation.surface: Choose a right-wing newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pick' looks like a verb, but it is the noun: the best of a group.
explanation.definitionFit: The pick of a bunch and the cream of the crop are both idioms for its very finest members.

clue.text: English given surprise about book, like A passage to India

indicators.note: about means around, so the word for surprise is wrapped round the book

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for English
to astound is to surprise greatly
B is the abbreviation for book

explanation.surface: An Englishman is surprised by a book, E M Forster's novel A Passage to India.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics make it look like the novel; read literally it is any voyage from Britain to India.
explanation.definitionFit: Travelling from Britain to India means heading in the direction of sunrise, so the voyage goes that way.

clue.text: Keep part of this dialect version?

indicators.note: a new version of a word can be a reworking of its letters into another order

blocks.note: the word taken as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: It reads as a question about whether a local form of speech is worth preserving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keep' looks like a verb meaning preserve, but it is the noun: a castle's central tower.
explanation.definitionFit: A keep is the strongest inner tower of a castle, and a citadel is likewise a fortress stronghold.

clue.text: Bay leaf initially included as spice

indicators.note: initially points to only the opening letter of leaf
included means taken inside, so the bay word holds the letter

blocks.note: a cove is a small bay
the opening letter of leaf

explanation.surface: A bay leaf goes into a dish as one of its seasonings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bay leaf' is a cooking herb, but the words split: bay is a coastal inlet.
explanation.definitionFit: A clove is the dried flower bud of a tropical tree, used whole or ground to flavour food.

clue.text: Girl supporting fierce person, one prominent in plot

indicators.note: in a down clue, a supporting element sits underneath, so the girl comes second

blocks.note: a tiger is a fierce, aggressive person
a girl's name

explanation.surface: A young woman backs a ferocious individual who is central to a conspiracy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plot' suggests a story or scheme; here it is a garden bed.
explanation.definitionFit: This tall orange spotted flower stands out in a garden bed, a plot of ground.

clue.text: Mild expletive about female's plan

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the expletive goes round the female

blocks.note: drat is a mild curse
F is the abbreviation for female

explanation.surface: Someone swears gently at a woman's scheme.
explanation.definitionFit: A draft is a preliminary version or outline of a document or design, a sketch or scheme.

clue.text: Catches girls hiding ring

indicators.note: something hiding an object keeps it inside, so the girls enclose the ring

blocks.note: lasses are girls, chiefly in Scotland and the north of England
a ring is round, the shape of the letter O

explanation.surface: Someone catches some girls trying to conceal a stolen ring.
explanation.definitionFit: A cowboy captures cattle by throwing a looped rope over them, the verb in its third person.

clue.text: Herries one of those with picture in gallery collection

definitions.note: Rogue Herries is the title character, so the name stands for the epithet before it

definitions.text: one of those with picture in gallery collection

blocks.note: first meaning: ... Herries, the hero of Hugh Walpole's novel of that name

blocks.clueFragment: one of those with picture in gallery collection
blocks.note: second meaning: a ...' gallery is the police collection of photographs of criminals

explanation.surface: A man called Herries seems to have his portrait hanging in an art gallery.
explanation.walkthrough: Rogue Herries (1930) is a historical novel by Hugh Walpole; a rogues' gallery is a file of police mugshots.
explanation.definitionFit: The novel's title names its hero by this epithet, and the police photo collection is called a gallery of such villains.

clue.text: Fellows return to inform on Club member

indicators.note: to return is to go back, so the word for fellows is read from its end

blocks.note: university fellows are dons
to grass is British slang for informing on someone to the police

explanation.surface: College fellows come back to report a member of their club to the authorities.
explanation.walkthrough: The Club is the Pickwick Club in Dickens's The Pickwick Papers; Augustus Snodgrass is one of its members.
explanation.definitionFit: Augustus Snodgrass, the poetic one, belongs to Mr Pickwick's club in Dickens's first novel.

clue.text: Wild, unlike Bianca's sister

blocks.note: first meaning: savage, impossible to bring under control
second meaning: Bianca's sister is Katharina in The Taming of the Shrew, who was tamed

explanation.surface: A wild woman is contrasted with the sister of someone called Bianca.
explanation.walkthrough: In Shakespeare's The Taming of the Shrew, Bianca's elder sister Katharina is the shrew that Petruchio tames.
explanation.definitionFit: A wild creature cannot be subdued, while Shakespeare's shrew Katharina was eventually brought to heel by her husband.

clue.text: Proportional representation?

blocks.note: surface reading: the electoral system where seats match the share of votes
setter's reading: a way of expressing one quantity in proportion to another, such as 3:1

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is a fixed political term, but read literally it is any way of showing a proportion.
explanation.definitionFit: A mathematical comparison of two amounts, written like 2:1, literally represents their relative proportion.

clue.text: Longs to be nameless for long time

indicators.note: being without a name means the abbreviation for name is dropped from the word

blocks.note: longs means yearns

explanation.surface: Someone longs to stay anonymous for a great while.
explanation.walkthrough: N is the standard abbreviation for name.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying something lasted years is the everyday idiom for a very lengthy period.

clue.text: Person behind the times showing reluctant diligence, perhaps

blocks.note: reluctant, in no hurry
a diligence was a French public stagecoach, an example of the vehicle

explanation.surface: Someone old-fashioned shows only grudging hard work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Diligence' looks like hard work, but it is also an old French stagecoach.
explanation.definitionFit: A British colloquial word for someone who lags behind or is old-fashioned and slow to keep up.

clue.text: A foreign hatred, without love, accepted by all

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the hatred word wraps round the love

blocks.note: un is French for a
animus is hostility or hatred
love is zero in tennis, the letter O

explanation.surface: An alien's hatred, lacking any love, which everyone shares.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like 'lacking', but here it means outside, an old sense crosswords often use.
explanation.definitionFit: A decision that is unanimous has every member's agreement, with no one dissenting.

clue.text: Run into a football team, experts at scoring

indicators.note: into means put inside, so the run letter goes within the article plus team

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for run in cricket scores
taken as written
Rangers is a Glasgow football club

explanation.surface: A player runs into a team of footballers who are skilled at getting goals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scoring' suggests goals; here it is writing a musical score.
explanation.definitionFit: Arrangers adapt music for particular instruments and voices, writing out an orchestration or musical score.

clue.text: One in eight is female

blocks.note: surface reading: a statistic, one in eight of some group being women
setter's reading: a member of a rowing eight, the crew boat, who is a woman

explanation.walkthrough: 'Eight' looks like a fraction, but an eight is a racing boat with eight rowers.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman who rows in a racing crew; an eight is the boat crewed by eight rowers.

clue.text: Well spaced-out arrangement for sesame?

blocks.note: first meaning: a military formation with wide gaps between the soldiers
second meaning: 'Open sesame' is the command that opens the cave in Ali Baba

explanation.surface: Seeds of sesame are laid out with plenty of space between them.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the second half is a play: the command given to sesame in the Ali Baba tale.
explanation.definitionFit: In drill, troops in this formation stand widely separated, and Ali Baba's magic phrase is a command beginning with the first word.

clue.text: Time to be involved in beginnings of organised Communist revolution?

indicators.note: beginnings means only the opening letter of each following word is kept
involved in means caught up inside, so the phrase goes among the letters

blocks.note: the first letters of these two words
taken as written
first letter of this word

explanation.surface: A call for the right moment to join a Communist uprising.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark nods to the Russian October Revolution of 1917, which fits the whole surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A month is a period of time, and this one gave its name to the Bolshevik seizure of power.

clue.text: Gets striker out in divided part of England

blocks.note: first meaning: in cricket, to york a batsman is to dismiss them with a ball pitched right at their feet
second meaning: the short form of Yorkshire, historically divided into three Ridings

explanation.surface: A worker on strike is removed in a split region of England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Striker' suggests an industrial dispute or football, but here it is the cricket batsman. Yorkshire, the English county, was split into North, East and West Ridings.
explanation.definitionFit: A yorker is a cricket delivery aimed at the batsman's toes, and the abbreviated county was famously split into Ridings.

clue.text: Silly goose accepts credit, noted skinflint

indicators.note: something silly is disordered, so the bird's letters are muddled
accepting something takes it in, so the bird's letters hold the credit

blocks.note: the word itself, letters to be rearranged
CR is the abbreviation for credit

explanation.surface: A foolish person takes out a loan, like a famous miser.
explanation.walkthrough: Ebenezer Scrooge is the miser of Dickens's A Christmas Carol.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens's Ebenezer Scrooge, the tight-fisted miser of A Christmas Carol, is the literary byword for meanness.

clue.text: Head in charge of subject

blocks.note: the head of something is its top
i/c is the abbreviation for in charge

explanation.surface: A head teacher put in charge of a school subject.
explanation.definitionFit: The subject of a talk or essay is the matter it discusses, its theme.

clue.text: Explorer put on a warm coat

blocks.note: Mungo Park, the Scottish explorer of the Niger
taken as written

explanation.surface: An explorer puts on a thick coat against the cold.
explanation.walkthrough: Mungo Park was an 18th-century Scottish explorer of West Africa.
explanation.definitionFit: A parka is a hooded, padded jacket originally worn in Arctic regions for warmth.

clue.text: Star gets best part, featured in Vincent's picture

definitions.note: a description of the thing rather than a synonym

blocks.note: the sun is our nearest star
the flower of something is its finest part, as in the flower of youth

explanation.surface: An actor wins the lead role in a film about Van Gogh.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Star gets best part' reads as film casting. Vincent van Gogh painted a famous series of Sunflowers.
explanation.definitionFit: Van Gogh's celebrated series of still lifes shows these tall yellow blooms in a vase.

clue.text: Offensively cutting item in second group of letters?

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for second
a word is a group of letters

explanation.surface: A rudely sarcastic remark appearing in the next batch of letters received.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Offensively cutting' sounds like a hurtful remark; it is a weapon used in attack.
explanation.definitionFit: A sword is a bladed weapon used for attacking, an offensive edge rather than a defensive one.

clue.text: Close pub

blocks.note: first meaning: nearby, in the neighbourhood
second meaning: a British drinker's regular pub near home

explanation.walkthrough: 'Close pub' sounds like a call to shut a bar; the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Something nearby is in the neighbourhood, and the British call the nearest regular bar by the same word.

clue.text: Unfurnished accommodation for girl going for a song

indicators.note: accommodation houses its occupant, so the girl's name lives inside the other word

blocks.note: an unfurnished room is bare
a girl's name

explanation.surface: An empty flat for a woman is being let very cheaply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going for a song' is the idiom for selling cheaply; split, it is a link plus the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A barcarole is a Venetian gondolier's boating song, or a piece of music imitating one.

clue.text: Relief work amounted to nothing

blocks.note: as in the bill came to ten pounds
nothing is zero, the letter O; 'to' finishes the phrase 'amounted to'

explanation.surface: Charity work for those in need ended up achieving nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Relief work' suggests aid for the needy; here it is carving in relief.
explanation.definitionFit: A cameo is a gem or shell carved so the design stands raised above the background, a kind of relief carving.

clue.text: Stretched and felt pain again?

blocks.note: re- is the prefix meaning again
to ache is to feel a dull pain

explanation.surface: Someone did their exercises and their muscles hurt once more.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the split is a pun: read the answer as RE-ACHED.
explanation.definitionFit: To reach is to extend an arm out, so stretched for something is the same verb sense in the past.

clue.text: Quiet rest for Hamlet, finally

blocks.note: first meaning: absence of sound
second meaning: Hamlet's dying words are 'The rest is ...'

explanation.surface: At last, some peace and quiet for the troubled Prince of Denmark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finally' looks like a last-letter instruction, but it points to Hamlet's final line.
explanation.definitionFit: Stillness without noise is the plain sense, and Shakespeare's prince ends his life calling what remains by this word.
